content:
A security shift handover is where unfinished risk either gets controlled properly or rolls straight into the next team. When the handover is vague, rushed or inconsistent, the incoming supervisor wastes time working out what still matters. That is where repeat incidents begin.

## Start the handover before the shift ends

Good handovers do not begin when two supervisors finally stand next to each other at the door. They begin earlier, while the outgoing team is still closing actions properly. Open incidents, patrol gaps, contractor activity, access-control problems, equipment faults and client requests should be noted before the final conversation starts.

If your current notes are inconsistent, tighten the writing standard first with your [security handover notes guide](/blog/how-to-write-better-security-handover-notes) and your [daily occurrence reporting process](/blog/how-to-write-a-better-security-daily-occurrence-report-with-ai). A stronger verbal handover depends on better written support.

## Cover the information the next shift actually needs

A useful security handover should answer a small number of operational questions clearly:

- what happened on this shift that still matters now

- what risk is still live

- what action has already been taken

- what still needs to happen, by whom, and by when

- what the next supervisor should check first

The Health and Safety Executive's [shift handover guidance](https://www.hse.gov.uk/humanfactors/topics/shift-handover.htm) stresses preparation, communication and cross-checking so responsibility transfers reliably rather than casually.

## Use both written and verbal communication

A written log on its own is not enough. A purely verbal handover is not enough either. A tighter process uses both.

The written element should give the structure. The verbal element should highlight judgement, urgency and anything that could be misunderstood if someone only reads the note later. HSE's wider [safety critical communications guidance](https://www.hse.gov.uk/humanfactors/topics/communications.htm) makes the same point: where the message really matters, one communication method is rarely enough.

## Separate facts, assumptions and next actions

Incoming teams need to know what is confirmed and what still needs checking. A weak handover mixes those together. A stronger handover separates them.

For example:

- Fact: rear gate alarm activated at 21:40 and was reset by site security

- Current position: no sign of forced entry found on first inspection

- Next action: incoming supervisor to recheck the loading bay perimeter at 22:30 and update the client if the alarm repeats

That discipline should also match your [incident reporting process](/blog/how-to-write-a-clear-security-incident-report-that-managers-can-act-on) so your wider reporting standard stays consistent.

## Build in a cross-check, not just a handoff

One of the most useful improvements is a short cross-check by the incoming supervisor before responsibility is fully accepted. That can include checking high-risk doors, reviewing any open incident references, confirming pending client communications and testing whether key equipment faults are still unresolved.

A handover is safer when the incoming team has a chance to question anything unclear before the outgoing team disappears.

## Use a repeat-incident lens

Some handovers fail because they only record the latest event. Better handovers also identify patterns. If the same access point keeps being left unsecured, if the same patrol blind spot keeps reappearing or if the same contractor keeps missing close-down steps, that should be flagged as a repeat issue.

This is where your [near miss reporting process](/blog/how-to-improve-security-near-miss-reporting) supports the handover. The next shift should not be discovering recurring problems as if they are new every time.

## A practical handover example

Imagine a retail distribution site finishing a late shift. The outgoing supervisor notes that one delivery bay shutter stuck twice, a visitor challenge at the staff entrance led to a management complaint, and one patrol route was shortened because of heavy vehicle movement. A weak handover says, "Shutter issue, visitor issue, patrol done late." A stronger handover says exactly what happened, what was checked, which issue is still live and what the next supervisor must verify first.

## Key takeaways

- Better handovers start before the shift ends, not at the last minute.

- The incoming team needs live risk, current status and clear next actions, not a long story.

- Written and verbal handovers should support each other.

- Cross-checking reduces the chance of silent misunderstanding.

- Repeat issues should be flagged so teams stop rediscovering the same problem.

## Tighten the process this week

Choose one handover point that regularly causes confusion and rewrite the structure around it. Then test whether the next supervisor can identify the live risk, the owner and the next action in under one minute.
